contextBefore.narration: This completely recontextualizes our understanding of magic in this book. We have seen the mechanical exploitative magic of Andrew and Jadis.
They manipulate. They destroy. They use others as tools. But Alan's magic is entirely organic.
He doesn't construct Narnia like a He calls it forth. He sings and the earth actively responds.

beats.narration: It's participation, not domination. The clash between these two types of power
is perfectly visualized. When Jadis realizes what is happening, she recognizes
Alen's song as a magic far deeper and older than her own, and she is terrified by it. She takes that iron bar from London, steps forward,
and throws it with all her supernatural strength directly at the lion's head. It hits him squarely between the eyes, and Alan doesn't even break his
stride. It doesn't flinch at all. The iron bar just falls into the newly created soil. And this is where the magic of Narnia flexes its true nature.
Because the soil of this new world is so saturated with the power of organic creation and growth, it forces the dead manufactured London metal
to grow. Right before their eyes, the iron bar sprouts branches of metal and grows into a living, flickering lampost.
It's a profound limitation on Jadis' power. She intended to inflict violence and destruction. But in a world governed by organic creation, even
a weapon of mechanical destruction is absorbed, subverted, and transformed into something that grows.
She cannot unmake what is being made here. So, she flees into the woods. Aslan continues his song, and the animals literally burst out of the
earth. Mounds of dirt swell up, and deer, panthers, and dogs shake the soil right from their coats. It is deeply solemn, majestic, awe
inspiring, which makes what Lewis does next so shocking. Really, right in the middle of this high fantasy creation epic, he just
drops a joke. A joke? Yeah. Alang gathers pairs of the animals and gives them the gift of consciousness.
He breathes on them and says, "Love, think, speak, be talking All right. And the very first thing we hear in this brand new
universe is the cab horse Strawberry looking around and saying, "But please, we don't know very much yet." It completely undercuts the tension.
And then when the animals pledge not to go back to their dumb ways, a jackaw yells out, "No fear." In the middle of a dead silence, and all the other animals start making
weird noises, trying to suppress their See, I used to think this was just Lewis being a bit too precious with his children's book audience.
Why undercut the majesty of creation with a bird making a poorly timed comment? Because humor is the ultimate proof of free will.
If the creation is merely solemn, silent, and terrified of its creator, it is a dictatorship. It's exactly the kind of world Jadis ruled in char.
That makes a lot of sense. By allowing the animals to laugh, and Alen explicitly tells them, laugh and fear not, he establishes that this universe is
built on joy. Laughter requires perspective, surprise, and a lack of fear. Which brings us to the emotional climax of the book.
Beat seven, The Apple and the Garden's Gate. Digory has been watching all of this, but the awe of creation hasn't erased the reality of his grief.
His mother is still dying in London. He has to walk up to this terrifying, magnificent lion. He knows he brought evil into this pristine world
on the very morning of its birth. And when he faces Alen, his first instinct is self-preservation. He tries to deflect.
He says, "It was my uncle Alen. He sent us out by magic But Alen doesn't let him hide behind Uncle Andrew's cruelty.
He asks low and deep, "You met the witch?" Digory realizes he is standing before a being who sees through every rationalization.
He has to take ownership of what a person does with power they cannot undo. He admits it. He struck the bell.
He chose his pride. He brought the witch. It's a moment of absolute vulnerability. And in that vulnerability, Digree's grief
overwhelms his fear. He begs Alen for something, anything, to cure his dying mother. He realizes he has no leverage.
He can't bargain with a god. He looks up, expecting to see a stern, unyielding face of judgment.
But he doesn't. He sees great shining tears standing in the
lion's eyes. Aslan says, "My son, my son, I know
grief is great. Only you and I in this land know that." Yet, we cannot overstate how important this moment is.
Think about the ancient gods of mythology or the stoic removed god that Jadis represents. Power in those paradigms means being untouched
by the suffering of mortals. But Alen, who is currently managing the birth of an entire cosmos, stops and weeps over the grief
of one human boy. The vulnerability of power is what separates the divine from the tyrannical. Empathy doesn't diminish his He legitimizes
it. But empathy also doesn't mean a magical quick fix. Alon doesn't just snap his fingers and cure Digor's mother, right?

contextAfter.narration: Healing requires active participation. Alen gives Digree a mission. You must travel far to the west to an enclosed garden on a steep hill
to retrieve a specific silver apple. That apple will be planted to grow a tree of protection that will keep the witch out of Narnia for centuries.
